code.title: Retry test with a fake HTTP controller

followUps:
Make the fake HTTP backend fail first, then succeed, and assert how many requests the service made. With HttpTestingController, call expectOne(url).flush(null, {status: 500, statusText: 'Server Error'}), then expectOne(url) again for the retry and flush real data.

If the service does retry({count: 2, delay: 1000}), wrap the test in fakeAsync and tick(1000) between attempts. Example: two 500s then a 200 means three requests and one emitted value; a fourth expectOne must throw. verify() proves no extra attempts.

A spy on HttpClient.get only proves that your code called a method; it skips the pipeline that really matters. With HttpTestingController the real HttpClient runs, so interceptors, params, headers, body serialisation and error mapping are all exercised.

A spy returns of(data) and silently ignores a wrong URL, a missing header, or a changed method. It also makes tests brittle: change get to request and every spy breaks although behaviour is the same.

verify() fails the test if any request is still open that you never matched with expectOne or match. That catches code that sends an extra, duplicated or forgotten request.

Example: the service should call /api/users once, but a bug calls it twice. Your test flushes one, and without verify() it passes. With verify() in afterEach it fails with the leftover URL. It does not catch requests that were already flushed.

A real browser has layout, real CSS, real events and many web APIs; jsdom is only a simulation of the DOM, so layout-dependent code silently behaves differently. Anything measuring size or position returns 0: getBoundingClientRect, offsetWidth and scrollHeight are all 0.

Missing or stubbed in jsdom: IntersectionObserver, ResizeObserver, matchMedia, real focus rules and CSS cascade (computed styles are partial). You add small polyfills or mocks, or run those few specs in Vitest browser mode. Keep a thin Playwright layer for true visual and layout checks.

Without zone.js, fakeAsync does not work because it relies on the zone to intercept timers. Replace it with the runner's fake timers: vi.useFakeTimers(), then vi.advanceTimersByTime(300), and restore real timers in afterEach.

For rendering, drive change detection yourself: await fixture.whenStable() after an action. Example: a 300 ms debounce is tested by typing, advancing 299 ms (nothing happened), then 1 ms (one call). The waiting logic is the same; only the clock tool changes.

Measure the same command on the same CI machine type, before and after, using several runs and the median, because single runs vary. Record total wall time, time to first result, and slowest tests, not just your laptop numbers.

Example: Karma 6 min 40 s versus Vitest 1 min 50 s over five runs is about 3.6 times faster. Also separate cold start (browser launch, compilation) from per-test time, since the saving often comes from skipping the browser start.

With OnPush, a component is only re-checked when an input reference changes through Angular's binding system, an event fires inside it, or it is marked dirty. Assigning comp.name = 'x' directly changes the field but never marks the view dirty, so detectChanges() does not update the DOM.

fixture.componentRef.setInput('name', 'x') goes through the same path as a template binding and marks the view dirty. The first detectChanges() after direct assignment may even work, which hides the problem until the second.

Use a host component when you must test the component as a parent really uses it: template bindings, content projection (<ng-content>), directives that need a template ref, or the public output name in (changed)="...".

Example: a card with a projected title is tested by a host with <app-card><h2>Hi</h2></app-card> and asserting the heading appears inside. For plain inputs and outputs, setInput and a spy are simpler and enough.

triggerEventHandler('click', {}) just calls the listener function with the object you give; no browser event happens. It skips bubbling, disabled handling, default actions and focus, so a disabled button still "works".

A real button.click() dispatches a genuine event: a disabled button ignores it, a form submit fires, and propagation to parents works. Prefer real DOM events; use triggerEventHandler only for non-DOM events like a child component's output.

Overlay content (menus, dialogs, select options) is rendered in a container at the end of body, outside your fixture, so a harness loader on the fixture cannot see it. Use TestbedHarnessEnvironment.documentRootLoader(fixture).

Example: const select = await loader.getHarness(MatSelectHarness); await select.open(); then const root = TestbedHarnessEnvironment.documentRootLoader(fixture); const opts = await root.getAllHarnesses(MatOptionHarness). Material harnesses like MatSelectHarness.getOptions() already handle this for you.

parallel() runs several harness reads in one go and waits for stability once, instead of after each call. It is faster and gives a consistent snapshot of the UI.

Example: const [a, b] = await parallel(() => [btn.getText(), input.getValue()]); That costs one stabilisation instead of two, and avoids reading the second value after the first call changed something.

Harnesses wait for the app to become stable before each call, so they skip the loading state by default. To see it, turn off auto change detection with await harness.forceStabilize() control: call fixture.autoDetectChanges(false) or use manualChangeDetection(async () => {...}).

Example: click Save inside manualChangeDetection, assert the spinner is shown, then flush the pending HTTP request and assert it is gone. A fake service with a controllable promise also works.

In version 19 effects became part of change detection: component effects run during change detection of their component, before its template, rather than as separate microtask-queued jobs. Root (service) effects run as a separate scheduled job.

For tests: component effects need fixture.detectChanges(), while root effects need TestBed.tick() (v20+) or flushEffects() (v17-19). Do not assume they run immediately after signal.set(); they never do.

model() is a two-way signal input. Test both directions: parent to child with setInput('value', 3), and child to parent by acting on the DOM, then reading the model signal or the bound parent value.

Example with a host: <app-counter [(value)]="count">. Click "+" in the child and assert host.count() became 4. This proves the valueChange output wiring, not just the internal signal.

A resource has states: loading, resolved, error. Provide a fake loader (or fake HTTP via the controller), then check the status and value at each step. Use TestBed.tick() or await fixture.whenStable() to let it run.

Example: before flush, res.isLoading() is true and res.value() is undefined. After flush(user) and a tick, res.value() is the user. Flush an error and assert res.error() is set. Also change the request signal and check a reload.

code.title: Virtual clock: testing a debounce without waiting

followUps:
Zone.js works by replacing browser APIs such as setTimeout and Promise.then with wrapped versions. Native async/await uses engine-internal promise machinery that cannot be patched, so the zone loses track of it.

That is why Angular CLI builds downlevel async/await to generators plus promises in zone-based apps. It is also a reason fakeAsync struggles with native await and why zoneless apps use different test tools.

A cold observable starts producing when subscribed (each subscriber gets its own run, like an HTTP request). A hot one runs independently and subscribers see only what happens after they join (like clicks).

In marbles, cold('a-b|') starts at subscription time, while hot('--a-b|') has fixed times, and ^ marks when you subscribe, so earlier values are missed. Use cold for inner calls like HTTP, hot for event streams.

Make the inner observable cold with a known duration, then assert its subscription timeline with expectSubscriptions(inner.subscriptions).toBe('^-!'). The ! marks an unsubscribe, which is what switchMap does to the older inner when a new value arrives.

Example: input a-b with inner cold('---r|'): the first inner subscribes at frame 0 and is cancelled at frame 2, so only one result appears. This proves stale responses are dropped.

(ab) takes 4 frames in the diagram: the group has 4 characters ( and ), a and b, and in run mode each character is one frame. Both values emit at the same time, the frame where the group begins.

So (ab)| means a and b at frame 0, then completion at frame 4, because the next character after the group starts at frame 4. This is a common source of off-by-N mistakes; counting characters is the safe rule.

Use cold when the observable represents work that begins on subscribe: an HTTP call, a timer, or a "search result" that appears 100 ms after being asked. Use hot when events happen regardless of subscribers: user input, a websocket, a Subject.

In a typeahead test, the search terms are hot(...) (the user types on their own schedule) and the API is cold('100ms r|') (each call takes 100 ms from when it is made).

Effects are a function from an action stream to an action stream, so test them as plain RxJS. Provide actions$ as a hot or cold marble, inject a fake service returning a cold observable, then compare the effect output with expectObservable(effect$).toBe(...).

Example: hot('-a', {a: load()}) and service cold('--b|', {b: data}) expect '---c' where c is loaded({data}). Wrap it in testScheduler.run so time is virtual.

code.title: Single refresh when many requests get 401

followUps:
Use a shared in-flight refresh. The first 401 starts one refresh and stores it; later 401s wait for that same one. The retried request is marked (for example with an HttpContext flag or a header) so a second 401 fails instead of refreshing again.

Test it: flush 401 for a refresh request itself and assert the user is logged out with no further requests. Flush 401 on the retry and assert exactly one refresh happened. verify() catches loops, since extra requests stay open.

HttpContext carries typed per-request flags (like SKIP_AUTH) from the caller to interceptors. Test it by making a request with http.get(url, {context: new HttpContext().set(SKIP_AUTH, true)}) and asserting on req.request.headers.

Example: with the flag set, expectOne(url).request.headers.has('Authorization') is false; without it, the header equals Bearer abc. Two tests cover both paths.

MSW is better when you want the tests to treat the network as a real server: it intercepts at the network level, so the same handlers work in unit tests, Storybook, E2E in the browser and local development.

It suits flows with many endpoints, realistic sequences and non-Angular code. HttpTestingController stays better for precise assertions on one service call (exact request count, headers, body) and has no extra dependency.

Create a component with a canDeactivate guard that asks confirm or opens a dialog service. Provide a fake dialog service whose answer you control: { confirm: () => of(false) }.

Test with RouterTestingHarness: navigate to the page, then navigate away and assert the URL did not change when the fake returns false, and did change when it returns true. Unit-test the guard function with runInInjectionContext for both answers.

Lazy routes need no special setup with the real router: harness.navigateByUrl('/admin') triggers the real loadComponent or loadChildren import and returns the loaded component. Await it and assert the DOM.

To check that something is lazy, assert the chunk is not loaded before navigation (for example, with a spy on the import wrapper). Keep these as a few wiring tests; the page logic is tested separately.

provideLocationMocks() replaces the browser Location with a fake, so navigations in tests do not touch the real URL or history. You can then check paths and simulate back with Location.back().

Since v15 the RouterTestingHarness with provideRouter works without it for most tests; you need the mock mainly to assert location.path() or test history behaviour like back navigation.

Template-driven forms (ngModel) set their values asynchronously, after a microtask, so the first detectChanges() shows an empty model. You must wait for fixture.whenStable() before reading or setting values.

Example: set comp.name = 'Ann', call detectChanges(), await whenStable(), detectChanges() again; only then does the input show Ann. Reactive forms update synchronously and do not need this.

updateOn: 'blur' delays copying the input text into the control until the field loses focus. Test it by typing (set value, dispatch input) and asserting the control value is still the old one, then dispatching blur and asserting it updated.

Example: after typing "abc" the control value is "" and valid is unchanged; after blur it is "abc" and validators have run once.

Check that each input has an accessible label, that errors are linked with aria-describedby and announced (role="alert"), invalid fields have aria-invalid="true", and focus moves to the first invalid field on failed submit.

Query by role and label, as in getByLabelText('Email'): if that fails, a screen reader user could not find the field either. An automated axe check adds a cheap safety net.

Build the app per pull request, deploy it to a preview URL (a container or static host), wait for a health check, then run Playwright with baseURL set from the preview address via an environment variable.

Seed data through the API per test, run against that isolated environment, upload the report and traces, and tear the preview down when the PR closes. Shard across jobs, for example 4 shards, to keep the feedback time under 10 minutes.

Download the trace artifact (Playwright trace viewer shows DOM snapshots, network and console at each step) and compare it with a local run. Check differences: slower CPU, different viewport, timezone, fonts, or data left by other tests.

Reproduce using the same container image, --workers=1 and CI env variables. Add trace: 'on-first-retry' and video so the next failure carries evidence instead of guesses.

Add visual regression for stable, high-value screens: design-system components, pricing and checkout pages, or anything where CSS bugs cost money. Do not add it for pages with dynamic content or constant redesign.

Keep it reliable by fixing viewport, fonts and animations, masking dates and ads, and storing baselines created in the same container as CI. Review diffs in the PR like code.

Say that coverage shows what code ran, not whether anything was checked. A test with no assertions gives 100% coverage and catches nothing, so chasing the number rewards weak tests.

Offer a concrete alternative: a threshold around 80% to stop decay, plus mutation testing on the pricing module. Example: one bug in discount logic cost more than the whole last quarter of low-value tests on getters.

The pyramid says many unit tests, fewer integration tests, very few E2E tests, because lower layers are faster and cheaper. The trophy (popular in front-end) puts most value on integration tests, with a base of static analysis.

For Angular, I follow the trophy: component tests with real templates and fake HTTP give the best confidence per minute. Keep pure logic unit-tested and E2E tiny. Both models agree on speed and cost.

Profile first: which specs and which stage (build, run, E2E) take the time. Typical fixes: run in parallel and shard, run only affected tests on PRs, cache dependencies and build output, and replace E2E with component tests.

Example: 40 min becomes about 10 by sharding E2E across 4 workers and running affected unit tests only. Run the full suite nightly and before release, not on every push.

code.title: Shard slow tests across workers (LPT)

followUps:
Run the suite many times in random order with a fixed seed printed in the output. If a failure appears, rerun with the same seed to reproduce it; then bisect by removing half the tests at a time until the failing pair remains.

Example: with 200 tests, about 8 halvings find the polluter. A polluter usually leaves behind a shared variable, a timer, localStorage, or an unfinished HTTP request.

Track a small set of numbers: flaky rate (same commit, different results), pass rate on the main branch, total and p95 duration, slowest 10 tests, retries used, and time to fix a quarantined test.

Example: flaky rate under 1%, quarantine list under 10 with owners, suite under 10 minutes. Plot them weekly so trends are visible.

Add checks to the pipeline: run new or changed tests 20 times in a loop on the PR, run the suite in random order, and fail on leaked timers or unhandled requests (verify()).

Add lint rules against fixed sleeps and fit/fdescribe, and require retries to be reported, never silent. A flaky test found on the PR is cheap; found on main it blocks everyone.
